en: *Shingon Yōketsu*, Scroll One.
Regarding the theft of [the Dharma]... [omitted] ...seeking favor and scheming for profit, amassing wealth.
[They treat] those of humble station with contempt and harbor hatred toward them.
He loves himself;
he squanders his wealth on horses, seeking out garments, ornaments, and luxurious articles of extravagant splendor.
He adorns his buildings and structures, allowing his will to run wild and his passions to run riot.
They practice and study empty words, regarding them as eloquence;
they cultivate clever deceptions, taking them for wisdom;
they act with arrogance and cruelty toward the poor and lowly, while flatteringly fawning upon the wealthy and noble.
They detest the upright and loathe the righteous; they envy the virtuous and good.
They protect their own shortcomings, gloss over their errors, and reject counsel.
They boast of their achievements and disparage the merits of others.
Those who share in evil associate with one another;
they form cliques and wander about in violence and arrogance.
They seek nourishment for their lives through the flavors of offerings, performing sacrifices to solicit blessings.
They perform incantations and curses to eliminate misfortune and petitions for the destruction of life.
They abandon the fundamental and pursue the peripheral, turning their backs on the correct and practicing the deviant.
They seek out shamans and spirit-mediums, placing their trust in sorcery and delusion.
They indulge in side-poems, flowery rhapsodies, colored paintings, and incense;
they devote themselves to heterodox doctrines, strange arts, gambling,
and licentious pleasures to delight their ears and eyes and to please women.
Addicted to pleasure as their constant pursuit, they remain unenlightened throughout their entire lives;
from those of mediocre intelligence downward, none are without this failing.
Day and night they toil in anxiety, never forgetting to sleep or eat.
Fathers and sons, brothers, harbor mutual estrangement and deception;
uncles and cousins, husbands and wives, treat one another with mutual suspicion and duplicity;
they shut their doors to practice internal instruction through deceit and oppression.
They open the gates and send others out to carry out their deeds;
they feign goodness and pretend intimacy while remaining estranged within and abandoning those outside.
They speak sweet words, force a smile, and maintain a gentle countenance with outward deference.
Their hearts lack compassion while their mouths abound with affection;
they do not consider it evil, and so they practice it together.
If they were to realize it is wrong, who would be willing to commit it again?
I believe that the Way is contrary to the mundane world and opposed to falsehood;
yet among those who practice the truth, there is not one in ten thousand,
while those who practice falsehood are as numerous as shoulders side by side.
Thus, the various heterodoxies mingle with the orthodox;
the orthodox is truly difficult to practice.
The multitude of falsehoods confuses the true.
Truth is difficult to discern;
thus, Confucius suffered the censure of Wushi,
and the Duke of Zhou faced the accusations of Guan and Cai.
Therefore, when the Way of the noble person declines, the perfected person withdraws into obscurity.
Were it not for those of brilliant wisdom, who else could awaken to this?
Thus, Zhuangzi said:
The words of ultimate truth do not emerge;
worldly speech excels them.
As a poem says:
Upon hearing words, they respond;
when reciting them, they are like one intoxicated.
Thus, the worldly mind is deluded in this manner.
How tragic this is!
Everyone desires that others love them,
yet no one desires to love others themselves.
Everyone detests others for their faults toward them,
yet no one detests themselves for their faults toward others.
Everyone loathes others for pointing out their shortcomings.
One does not resent others for pointing out one's faults;
everyone desires that others' conduct be trustworthy toward oneself,
yet one does not desire that one's own conduct be trustworthy toward others.
Everyone desires that others' conduct be upright toward themselves,
yet they do not desire their own conduct to be upright toward others.
When poor, everyone desires that others show them kindness with wealth.
When wealthy, they do not take pleasure in bestowing their riches upon others;
when in peril themselves, they desire others to rescue them;
yet when others are in peril, they are unwilling to save them with their own person.
Regarding one's own wife and concubines, one does not wish for others to gaze upon them;
yet, seeing the wives and concubines of others, one delights in licentiousness with a lustful mind.
Regarding one's own parents, one desires that others show them reverence and honor.
Upon seeing the parents of others, they are unwilling to humble themselves to show them respect;
instead, they spend their days tirelessly harboring resentment toward their peers,
failing to know how to turn inward to reproach themselves or examine their own conduct.
Since they do not comprehend the nature of coming and going,
they are no different from birds and beasts.
Therefore, the *Liji* says:
If a human being lacks ritual propriety, even if they are eloquent in speech,
do they not possess the mind of a bird or beast?
Thus spoke Confucius.
If one is self-exacting and lenient in holding others accountable, one will remain far removed from resentment.
People of the world know only to discuss the shortcomings of others,
yet fail to recognize their own lack of virtue.
They only know to criticize others' sons for lacking benevolence and wisdom,
yet do not realize their own sons are mediocre and foolish;
they only know to criticize others' wives for having lewd conduct.
They do not realize that their own wives lack a heart of constancy and sincerity;
they only know to laugh at others for lacking propriety and righteousness.
They do not realize that they themselves lack human feeling.
One only knows how to resent others for not paying one respect,
yet does not know that one possesses nothing worthy of knowledge;
one only knows how to discuss others' meanness and stinginess, yet does not know one's own.
Not realizing that one is oneself stingy and greedy,
those who wish to discuss the affairs of others should first examine their own bodies.
Those who wish to laugh at the faults of others should first examine their own strengths and weaknesses; if they do not do so,
[they will find no cause for laughter].
How, then, could this be called "mediocre wisdom"? Thus, the *Yì* says,
"Returning [to the source] through self-knowledge," and Lǎozǐ says,
"He who knows himself is enlightened."
This is precisely what is meant by that.
To hear of one's faults and not immediately reform them is the mark of a fool;
to see the whip and not immediately move forward is the mark of a feeble horse.
A hack horse is spurred and whipped all day long;
a fool is reviled and humiliated all day long.
Is one who, despite being reviled and humiliated, remains ignorant of shame any more base than a hack horse?
Therefore, the *Śāsanānuśāsanī Sūtra* says:
"If one lacks a sense of shame, there is no difference between such a person and the birds and beasts.
The *Book of Changes* (*Yijing*) says:
The gentleman shifts toward what is good upon seeing it and reforms when he has faults; therefore,
the Buddha-dharma permits the disclosure and repentance of transgressions.
The royal law permits one to confess a fault by acknowledging it;
if the disclosure of the matter is incomplete, the confession cannot be accomplished.
If the acknowledgment of the matter is incomplete, the confession of the fault cannot be accomplished.
Therefore, one who repents and reforms their transgressions must reveal them with complete sincerity;
one who confesses and acknowledges their faults must set forth the circumstances in full detail.
If, after repenting, one commits further offenses...
If one does not repent, there is no escape;
to acknowledge past faults yet create further transgressions is insufficient.
If one does not confess, there is no escape.
Therefore, one who acknowledges their primary transgressions must purify their will so that it is renewed daily;
one who practices repentance must cleanse their mind so that it remains constantly unified.
This is why Yan Hui did not repeat his mistakes.
The Master esteemed this;
hence the Book says:
"When virtue is single-minded, every movement will be auspicious."
If one's virtue is divided between two courses, every action will be ominous.
The *Yi* says:
"The *Heng* hexagram consists in the constancy of a single virtue," for such is the firmness of constant virtue.
The candle-maker seeks its light;
the scripture-reader seeks its principle.
Light is used to illuminate the dark room.
Principle uses illumination to dispel the dark mind;
therefore, even if one creates a candle, it cannot burn [the darkness].
Though the candle exists, the darkness is not eliminated.
If one reads the scriptures but does not perceive their underlying principle,
though one reads them, one's folly will not cease.
It is like being in a dark room where movement meets obstruction.
When the mind is deluded and moves, transgressions arise.
The arising of transgressions is due to a lack of wisdom;
the presence of obstructions is due to a lack of illumination.
Therefore, worldly people only know to make candles and seek light to illuminate their rooms;
they do not understand how to read the scriptures and seek principle to illuminate their minds.
How foolish they are!
When the strings of a lute or zither are tuned, one who plays them will master the melodies;
one for whom they are not tuned will merely produce empty sounds.
When the scriptures are explained, one who reads them will grasp their underlying principles.
Those who do not understand read them and obtain nothing but their words.
Thus, although the deaf may listen to the lute and the zither, they never hear the sound of the lute and zither;
likewise, although the foolish may read the scriptures, they never perceive the principles of the scriptures.
Therefore, the *Liji* says:
"There are none among men who do not eat and drink, yet few are able to know their flavors.
This is precisely what that refers to.
Though the scriptural teachings are numerous,
those who understand their principles grasp their profound meaning;
though the river waters are vast, [those who know how to cross find the ford].
Those who distinguish the waters perceive its deep current;
those who perceive its deep current board a boat and reach the further shore;
those who grasp its profound meaning direct their minds and transcend birth and death.
One sets a net in order to seek turtles and fish.
Since turtles and fish dwell in deep water,
merely setting a net does not mean one has entered the water to catch fish with it.
He then bound them together and hung them high,
so that neither turtles nor fish could reach them;
he composed this scripture to seek merit and wisdom.
Merit and wisdom reside within the profound mind.
Having produced this scripture, he did not read or recite it,
but instead bound his mind with a net and placed it within a casket.
Merit and wisdom have no means of arising;
furthermore, one who reads the scriptures without attaining their profound principles is like spreading a net in the air and dragging it through water.
They spread their nets, dragging them empty through the water;
in vain the nets were soaked and the men exhausted,
yet not a single turtle or fish was caught.
Those who read the scriptures but do not grasp their profound principles merely grow weary of the paper while their minds remain indolent;
they achieve nothing at all in terms of merit or wisdom.
Ordinary people all understand that once a fishing net has been woven, they enter the water to seek fish;
yet those who have composed a scripture do not know to recite it to seek its underlying principle,
knowing only that fish are caught by baiting them with excrement.
Those who do not know how to govern by means of the "Manure God" seek to govern through the Manure God;
such seekers roam together with the Way and its Virtue.
Those who seek fish by manuring their bodies share the same inclinations as birds and beasts.
Those whose inclinations are equal to those of birds and beasts, though possessing human form,
constantly harbor the minds of animals;
those who roam together with the Way and its Virtue, though they be ordinary persons.
One should always maintain the conduct of a bodhisattva.
The conduct of a bodhisattva is to benefit sentient beings;
the mind of a beast is solely for mutual plundering and exploitation.
One who plunders the mind will surely engage in a quarrel over a single coin;
one who practices beneficial conduct will never contend over ten thousand pieces of gold.
Though their material circumstances may be identical, their mental dispositions and actions differ vastly.
To compare their relative merits and shortcomings is beyond the reach of analogy.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Though his body is that of a man, his conduct is identical to that of a beast."
Although one may receive a human body and mind like the mind of a Buddha,
it is like a blind man steering a boat to the other shore;
unable to see the course of the water, he will eventually run aground on a sandbar.
The fool reads the scriptures seeking blessings, yet the wise man,
unable to understand their underlying meaning, ultimately incurs transgression;
like a blind man walking onto a sandbar, he does not perceive his own peril.
The fool commits offenses without realizing it;
being unaware, he sees the boat and sees himself in the water,
yet the body of the boat remains the same whether moving or staying still.
Therefore, when the enlightened ones instruct them, they ultimately do not believe.
Those who lack self-awareness perceive only their own bodies and focus on reading the scriptures;
yet the essence of the scriptures, whether profound or shallow, is of one and the same nature.
Therefore, the wise inform them [of the truth], yet they never rely upon it.
Thus we know that one who distinguishes waters cannot guide a blind man’s boat,
and one who understands principle cannot awaken the wisdom of a fool.
If a blind person accepts guidance, they will surely reach the other shore;
if a fool accepts instruction, they will surely transcend birth and death.
This is universally known by all: when a blind man seeks to cross the water, he must board a boat.
In the end, they do not realize that the ignorant seek the principles of liberation while those who know the Way ask about it.
Consequently, while alive they are filled with anxiety and a hundred anxieties;
when dead, they transmigrate through the three miserable realms.
How bitter it is!
The *Analects* says:
"When one says 'What can be done? What can be done? I have no further means to help."
When a woman is pregnant with a child, she cannot help but give birth;
once born, it cannot help but die.
It is just as when one is hungry, one cannot help but eat.
Once one has eaten, one cannot avoid excreting;
once one has excreted, the failure to do so becomes a source of affliction for the body.
Since death is inevitable yet one does not die [of this], how could this be auspicious?
Therefore, there has never been food that does not come forth,
nor has there ever been a person who does not die;
it is only that their emergence and passing occur at different times.
Lives have varying lengths;
the distinction between superior and inferior among them is not worth considering.
Therefore, if the previous meal has not been digested, how could the subsequent meal enter?
If one does not die in a previous life, how can one be born in a subsequent life?
The world universally knows that for those who eat, digestion occurs according to its own time;
yet it fails to realize that for those who are born, death occurs according to its own time.
This is also one of his delusions.
Thus, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra says:
"I originally did not crave birth."
Nor do they delight in death;
with single-mindedness and wisdom,
they wait for the time to come before departing.
A mirror is used to reflect the face;
wisdom is used to reflect the mind.
Therefore, when a mirror is bright, dust and grime do not remain upon it.
When wisdom is clear, desire and evil do not arise.
A person who lacks the Way is like a carriage without an axle;
a carriage without an axle cannot be driven.
If a person lacks the Way, they cannot act rightly.
When a person does not hear the Way on a small scale,
their desires and aversions will inevitably uproot and injure their nature.
It is like rice that has not been weeded when young;
the weeds and tares will surely overwhelm and stifle its sprouts.
Even if it has emerged and flourished, if it is not weeded and cultivated, [it will perish].
Those who attain the reality will surely be few;
those who hear the Way in old age will not obtain much of the truth.
One whose roof is broken is constantly afraid of wind and rain;
one whose mind is crooked is constantly anxious about calamities and misfortunes.
Therefore, once the roof is repaired, wind and rain cannot enter his house.
When one’s mind is correctly aligned, calamities cannot enter it.
The world universally knows how to patch a roof to ward off wind and rain,
yet it does not know how to rectify the mind to eliminate calamities.
How foolish this is!
Thus Laozi said:
"Cultivate it within one's own person, and its virtue will become truly authentic."
Those who possess wings that soar toward the heavens will certainly not alight upon the fading light of the setting sun.
Those whose minds dwell beyond the mundane world will certainly not discourse upon fame and profit.
Therefore, those who speak of fame and profit are petty people of shallow ambition.
Those who discourse on the Way are men of noble character with profound insight.
Therefore, while the petty person takes fame and profit as their primary concern,
the man of noble character takes the Way and its Power as his mainstay.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"The gentleman understands righteousness;
the petty person understands profit."
When white jade is cast into black mud, it cannot be defiled or destroyed in its color;
when a gentleman wanders through a turbid world, he cannot be stained or disordered in his mind.
Therefore, the pine and cypress can bear frost and snow.
Wisdom enables one to traverse hardships and calamities.
Only after the cold of winter does one know the luxuriance of the pine and cypress.
Only when the world is turbid does one know the penetration of the Perfected Man.
If one throws a stubborn stone into a river, it will not be moistened for ten thousand years;
if one assembles foolish people to speak of the Way, they will not hear it for their entire lives.
Therefore, the *I Ching* says:
"To know the subtle signs—is this not divine?
The eyes perceive forms;
the mind illuminates principles."
Therefore, when the eyes are circumspect, one's steps do not injure the feet;
when the will is tranquil, movement does not weary the spirit.
When the walls and buildings are solidly secured from without, evil persons cannot enter the chamber.
When one's virtue is firm within, depraved influences cannot invade the mind.
When a family is wealthy, others do not seek from them at a distance.
When one’s aspirations are fulfilled, the mind does not turn toward external attachments.
Those who are free from illness do not seek out skilled physicians;
those who have no desires do not scheme for honor and favor;
those who have cast off greed do not prize gold and jade.
One who has renounced fame does not desire either defamation or praise;
one who delights in the Way and finds contentment in poverty will not be visited by friends seeking wealth;
one who embraces virtue while dwelling in solitude will not be sought after by those driven by power and profit.
Those who accumulate grain and silk do not worry about hunger or cold;
those who embrace the Way and its Virtue do not fear misfortune or evil.
In this world, everyone understands the practice of storing grain and silk as a means to prevent hardship and insufficiency.
Failing to understand how one should cherish the Way and its Virtue to prepare for hardships and calamities,
Confucius continued to play the strings and sing even while between Chen and Cai.
The *I Ching* says:
Though one may be in distress,
there is penetration. To speak of cravings and desires while failing to speak of the Way and its Power is because of the absence of True Suchness (Tathatā).
They eat dregs and coarse grain rather than rare delicacies because they lack rice and millet;
they wear hempen and flaxen garments rather than fine silks because [they lack such materials].
This is because they have no silk or cotton for clothing.
They walk with staffs and sandals rather than riding fat horses,
because they have no carriages to ride.
The world universally seeks chariots and cavalry to replace walking on foot;
seeks silk and cotton to replace hemp and flax;
and seeks fine rice and grain to replace dregs and husks.
Failing to understand how to cultivate true wisdom to eliminate craving and desire,
one suffers insatiable longing that leads to the loss of body and life—
is this not indeed folly?
To speak of the Way and its virtue without practicing them is like being hungry but not eating;
to practice the Way without finding joy in it is likewise so.
One who finds pleasure in the Way but does not persevere to the end is like one who eats food that is sweet but does not find it satisfying.
One who eats with relish but is not satiated is likewise.
Therefore, when one finds joy in the Way to its conclusion, the spiritual intelligence becomes expansive;
when one partakes of sweet food until satiated, the physical form and vital energy become full.
Thus, people of the world know only to use food to fill their physical form and vital energy.
They do not know to exalt the spirit through the Way and its Virtue.
Now, when the spirit is exhausted while the physical form remains full, it is like a minister who is strong and the ruler who is weak;
when the minister is strong and the ruler is weak, the state will surely fall into ruin.
When the form is full but the spirit is withered, the body will surely die;
those whose words are sycophantic lack true conduct,
while those who harbor purity have no need for ornate rhetoric.
Those with excessive lust delight in floral adornments;
those with excessive profit delight in socializing.
Therefore, one whose social circle is vast lacks sincerity of heart.
Those whose adornments are sumptuous lack integrity of will;
therefore, those with integrity of will wear coarse clothing,
and those whose hearts are sincere prefer simple friendships.
If one observes others by this standard, there will not be a single failure out of ten thousand.
Therefore, the *Yi* says:
"To cultivate a refined appearance is to encourage licentiousness."
The *Book of Rites* (*Liji*) says:
"The friendship of the gentleman is like water.
Laozi says:
Truthful words are not beautiful;
beautiful words are not truthful.
When speech is verbose, it lacks substance, and the underlying principle is obscured.
Those who overthink gain no benefit and their minds grow weary;
filial sons nourishing their parents forget all toil and suffering;
true persons embracing the Way cast aside their physical forms.
Therefore, one does not select tasks before acting because of the desire to nourish one's parents;
one does not select locations before settling because of the longing for the Way.
Thus, Confucius said:
In eating, he did not seek satiety;
in his dwelling, he did not seek comfort.
Thus, the Confucian scholar would bend his arm and dwell in a humble alley.
The Way involves serenely sitting amidst mountain forests;
a virtuous woman does not marry without a worthy matchmaker;
and the ultimate truth is not proclaimed without truthful speech.
A skilled matchmaker will certainly not falsely propose for her daughter;
one who speaks truth will certainly not utter false words.
A matchmaker does not falsely propose, but rather proposes on the basis of her actual virtues.
When one speaks without falsehood, one expresses the actual principle;
when one mediates based on actual virtue, those seeking marriage are not deluded.
When one speaks according to actual principle, those who listen do not doubt.
Without doubt, she will surely receive and practice [the teachings];
without confusion, she will surely accept them to become the mistress of the household.
Thus, when a family obtains a compliant wife, they can bring peace and harmony to the nine branches of their kin.
When the mind attains the true principle, the hundred members of the body can be tranquil and at ease;
when the nine clans are peaceful and harmonious, the branches and leaves flourish outwardly.
When the hundred members are tranquil and at ease, the seed-wisdom (*tathāgata-garbha*) is illuminated within.
When their branches and leaves flourish outwardly, they are renowned as a powerful clan;
when their knowledge of all modes of wisdom shines inwardly, they are called men of realization.
Therefore, worldly people only know how to seek out a skilled matchmaker to inquire after the virtues of a wife.
Not knowing to seek out truthful words and inquire after their ultimate meaning—
how foolish this is!
Therefore, Confucius said:
If one chooses not to dwell in benevolence, how can they be considered wise?
If medicine does not correspond to the illness, it is no different from not taking it at all;
if words do not hit upon the principle, it is no different from not speaking at all.
When medicine does not suit the illness, it conversely harms one's life;
when speech does not accord with principle, it conversely injures oneself.
Thus, the *Yi* says:
The origin of disorder is that speech serves as its ladder.
Laozi said:
"If one opens the gates of the senses and pursues their affairs, there will be no salvation for the rest of one's life."
When fools take a wife, they do not seek her virtue;
they take as their primary standard only the family lineage, wealth, status, and physical beauty.
When a woman relies on her looks, she will inevitably give rein to arrogance and lust.
Relying on their family lineage, they will surely harbor arrogance and contempt;
being arrogant and contemptuous, they will be disobedient toward their parents-in-law;
being haughty and lustful, they will be led astray by the seductions of others.
If one does not obey their parents-in-law, then harmony will not prevail between the inner and outer families.
If one is seduced and deluded by others, then both outwardly and inwardly they will become turbid and licentious, indulging in lust.
The foolish person never awakens to this realization.
Furthermore, fearing she might be slighted or treated with disdain by her husband, she will resort to every possible means;
she seeks out shamans and performs exorcisms,
neglecting the duties of a wife, thinking only of music, beauty, fine clothing, and elegant makeup.
The sycophantic husband-in-law uses deceit to feign intimacy;
he slanders those of high and low station,
and the husband accepts the words of his wife.
They treat their own flesh and blood with neglect and coldness,
causing their closest kin and those of the same breath to harbor grievances that pierce the heavens.
Of such people as these, there are surely not merely three or five.
To endanger one’s person and sacrifice one’s life is truly the way of women;
that states are lost and families ruined all stems from female beauty.
Therefore, during the height of King Wen’s prosperity, he first extolled the virtue of his consort.
When King Zhou of Yin perished, he ultimately attributed his transgressions to Daji;
as for the other petty courtiers, they are beyond counting.
How can one fail to realize the danger of the "hen crowing at dawn"?
Therefore, the Odes say:
"The wife has a long tongue; it is the very step of calamity. Disorder does not descend from Heaven; it arises from women.
If there is no sameness, then there is no difference.
Where there is no union, there is no separation;
where there is no gathering, there is no dispersal;
where there is no love, there is no hatred.
Where there is no sorrow, there is no joy;
where there is no gain, there is no loss;
where there is no birth, there is no death.
Where there is no intimacy, there is no estrangement.
In this world, there are those who were first strangers and later became close,
and there are those who were first close and later became strangers.
As for a husband and wife who have not yet been united and do not know one another,
they are initially estranged;
yet once they have married, they share a heart of affection and love.
Thus, those who are close by blood are later relatives;
brothers of the same womb who share the same vital breath are earlier relatives.
Later, they eventually became estranged; thus,
what was originally distant became like glue and lacquer between husband and wife.
Brothers who were originally one have now become like strangers; moreover,
they glare at one another with hostility, harboring hatred, resentment, and jealousy,
each scheming for his own sake while providing for his wife and children.
Not only do they disregard the kindness of their parents, but they also harbor a craving for wealth and sensual beauty.
As this habituation persists for a long time, it eventually becomes their constant way of life;
thus it is with the entire world.
Who, then, can be considered close or distant?
Therefore, those who associate for the sake of wealth become distant as soon as their wealth is exhausted;
those who associate for the sake of beauty are abandoned as soon as their beauty fades.
Those who associate for the sake of food part as soon as the food is exhausted;
those who associate for the sake of reputation sever ties as soon as the reputation vanishes;
those who associate for the sake of power drift apart as soon as the power departs.
Those who associate through artifice sever their bond once that artifice is exhausted.
Therefore, those who unite for a specific reason must inevitably have a reason to separate;
whereas those who are united without such a reason will necessarily remain without cause for discord.
That which exists because it is not eternal is subject to occasional conjunction and disjunction;
that which does not exist because it is eternal has no occasion for identity or difference.
"Non-existence" refers to the union with the Path.
"Those who have [a reason] for being so refer to worldly relations.
Thus, the petty person has no kin unless there is a mutual benefit;
the superior man has no kin unless there is a commonality in the Way."
Those who do not share the Way do not associate; without the Way, they disperse.
Those who do not share mutual benefit do not join together; without mutual benefit, they part ways.
Thus, the *Book of Rites* says:
The Confucians agree in their principles but differ in their advancement and retreat.
Zhuangzi says:
"The superior man is detached yet intimate."
That "the petty person delights in severance" is indeed not erroneous.
Joy does not equal the endurance of insult.
Much laughter does not equal the absence of anger;
sparing life surpasses the act of releasing captive animals;
and seeking blessings is not as effective as avoiding transgressions.
Freedom from stinginess surpasses material giving;
a respectful mind surpasses formal courtesy.
Thus, the *Śāriputra-parivarta* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) says:
The virtue of patience cannot be equaled by the observance of precepts or the practice of asceticism.
One who is able to practice patience may truly be called a powerful great person.
It is further said:
"Nothing surpasses anger as a thief that plunders merit throughout the kalpas.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If someone inflicts evil upon one, it is like a pig rubbing against a mountain of gold; it only causes its brilliance to shine forth even more."
For those seeking the Buddha-way to deliver sentient beings,
patience is the most wondrous of sharp tools.
It is further said:
Hatred is the causal condition for suffering;
loving-kindness is the causal condition for happiness.
Zhuangzi said:
One who possesses strength equal to ten thousand men is not considered a true hero;
one who can practice even a single act of forbearance is called a great man.
The *Analects* says:
"To forget one's own person and even one's parents out of a momentary fit of anger—
is this not delusion?
The Way is fundamentally intended for the propagation of the Way and the transformation of all things."
This is not because of shaving one's head, wearing a cap, eating only vegetables, reciting sutras, prostrating before the Buddha, or practicing with a sincere heart;
for the office of an official is fundamentally intended to assist the state and govern the people.
This is because he does not harbor talent while occupying office and drawing a salary, nor is he pure and prudent in examining cases or adjudicating matters, but instead strikes people.
Therefore, Confucius said:
